The brachial plexus supplies the upper limb, the ulnar nerve supplies the hand, and the diaphragm is skeletal muscle that contracts only when its nerve fires.

labels.name: Axillary nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus branch that wraps behind the upper end of the humerus. It moves the deltoid, which lifts the arm out to the side, and carries feeling from the skin over the shoulder.

labels.name: Median nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus nerve that runs down the middle of the arm and forearm and through the wrist into the palm. It moves most of the muscles that bend the wrist and fingers and the muscles of the thumb, and carries feeling from the thumb side of the palm.

labels.name: Radial nerve
labels.fn: The largest branch of the brachial plexus. It winds around the back of the humerus and supplies the muscles that straighten the elbow, wrist and fingers, plus skin on the back of the arm and hand.

follow.q: A break through the middle of the humerus leaves a patient unable to lift the wrist and fingers (wrist drop). Which nerve was most likely injured?
follow.why: The radial nerve winds around the back of the middle of the humerus and supplies the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers, so a break there can stretch or cut it. The median and ulnar nerves mostly bend the wrist and fingers, and the axillary nerve supplies the shoulder.

labels.name: Ulnar nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus nerve that passes behind the inner bump of the elbow (the "funny bone") into the hand. It supplies most of the small muscles of the hand and the skin on the little finger side.

labels.name: Lumbar plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of L1 to L4. Its main branches, the femoral and obturator nerves, supply the front and inner thigh.

labels.name: Femoral nerve
labels.fn: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It enters the front of the thigh, moves the quadriceps, which straighten the knee, and carries feeling from the front of the thigh.

labels.name: Obturator nerve
labels.fn: A lumbar plexus nerve that leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen. It moves the muscles that pull the thigh inward and carries feeling from the skin of the inner thigh.

labels.name: Sacral plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of L4 to S4. It supplies the buttock, the back of the thigh, all the muscles below the knee and most of the skin there, mainly through the sciatic nerve.

labels.name: Common fibular nerve
labels.fn: The branch of the sciatic nerve that wraps around the top of the fibula just below the knee, where it lies close to the skin. It moves the muscles that lift the foot and toes, so damage there causes foot drop.

labels.name: Sciatic nerve
labels.fn: The largest nerve in the body, from the sacral plexus (L4 to S3). It runs down the back of the thigh, moves the hamstrings, and above the knee splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

follow.q: An injection placed too low and too close to the middle of the buttock can injure which nerve, weakening the back of the thigh and everything below the knee?
follow.why: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner part of the buttock and supplies the hamstrings and all the muscles below the knee. Injections avoid the buttock and use the ventrogluteal site on the side of the hip instead. The femoral and obturator nerves supply the front and inner thigh, and the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm.

labels.name: Tibial nerve
labels.fn: The branch of the sciatic nerve that continues down the back of the leg. It moves the calf muscles that point the foot and the muscles of the sole, and carries feeling from the sole.

labels.name: C5 dermatome
labels.fn: The C5 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C5. Its standard landmark is the skin over the outer side of the upper arm.

labels.name: C6 dermatome
labels.fn: The C6 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C6. Its standard landmark is the thumb. Across the hand, C6 is the thumb, C7 the middle finger and C8 the little finger.

follow.q: A patient has numbness of the thumb only. Which spinal nerve root is most likely involved?
follow.why: The thumb lies in the C6 dermatome. C8 covers the little finger side of the hand, T1 the inner forearm, and L5 the top of the foot.

labels.name: C7 dermatome
labels.fn: The C7 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C7. Its standard landmark is the middle finger.

labels.name: C8 dermatome
labels.fn: The C8 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C8. Its standard landmark is the little finger.

labels.name: T4 dermatome
labels.fn: The T4 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve T4. Its standard landmark is the chest at the level of the nipples. The thoracic dermatomes run as horizontal bands around the trunk.

labels.name: T10 dermatome
labels.fn: The T10 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve T10. Its standard landmark is the navel.

follow.q: After an injury to the spinal cord, a patient has lost feeling from the level of the navel down. At about which segment is the injury?
follow.why: The navel is the T10 landmark, so feeling lost from the navel down points to a cord injury at about T10. T4 is the nipple line, L1 the groin, and C8 the little finger.

labels.name: L1 dermatome
labels.fn: The L1 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L1. Its standard landmark is the groin.

labels.name: L4 dermatome
labels.fn: The L4 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L4. Its standard landmark is the inner side of the leg just below the knee.

labels.name: L5 dermatome
labels.fn: The L5 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L5. Its standard landmark is the top of the foot and the big toe.

follow.q: Pressure on one nerve root in the lower back causes numbness on the top of the foot and the big toe. Which root is affected?
follow.why: The top of the foot and the big toe form the L5 dermatome. S1 covers the outer edge of the foot and the little toe, L1 the groin, and C7 the middle finger.

labels.name: S1 dermatome
labels.fn: The S1 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve S1. Its standard landmark is the outer edge of the foot and the little toe.

sets.title: Cranial nerves on the inferior brain

labels.name: Olfactory nerve I
labels.fn: Cranial nerve I, purely sensory. Its fibers run from the lining high in the roof of the nose up into the skull to the underside of the frontal lobe and carry the sense of smell.

labels.name: Oculomotor nerve III
labels.fn: Cranial nerve III, a motor nerve from the midbrain. It moves most of the muscles that turn the eye, raises the upper eyelid, and through parasympathetic fibers makes the pupil smaller.

follow.q: A patient's right eye rests turned down and out, the right upper eyelid droops and the right pupil is wide. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
follow.why: The oculomotor nerve moves most eye muscles, lifts the eyelid and narrows the pupil, so losing it leaves the eye pulled down and out by the two muscles it does not supply, a drooping lid and a wide pupil. The trochlear and abducens nerves each move one eye muscle and do not touch the lid or pupil, and the facial nerve closes the eye rather than opening it.

labels.name: Optic nerve II
labels.fn: Cranial nerve II, purely sensory. It carries vision from each eye back into the brain; the two optic nerves meet beneath the brain, where some of their fibers cross to the other side.

labels.name: Trochlear nerve IV
labels.fn: Cranial nerve IV, the smallest cranial nerve and the only one leaving the back of the brainstem (the midbrain). It moves the one eye muscle that turns the eye down and slightly out. Its downward pull is strongest when the eye points toward the nose, so you test it by looking down and in.

labels.name: Trigeminal nerve V
labels.fn: Cranial nerve V, a mixed nerve from the pons. Its three branches carry touch, pain and temperature from the face, the front of the scalp, the mouth and the inside of the nose, and its motor fibers work the chewing muscles.

follow.q: Which cranial nerve carries touch and pain from the skin of the face?
follow.why: The trigeminal nerve is the main sensory nerve of the face. The facial nerve, despite its name, mainly moves the face, the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue, and the vagus nerve serves the throat and the organs of the chest and abdomen.

labels.name: Abducens nerve VI
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VI, a motor nerve that leaves where the pons meets the medulla. It moves the one eye muscle that turns the eye outward.

labels.name: Facial nerve VII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VII, a mixed nerve from the lower pons. It moves the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, and drives tear and saliva secretion.

follow.q: A patient cannot close her left eye or smile on the left, and food tastes dull on the front of the left side of her tongue. Which nerve is affected?
follow.why: The facial nerve moves the muscles of facial expression, including the one that closes the eye, and carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, so one lesion explains both. The trigeminal nerve carries touch from the face and works the chewing muscles, the glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue, and the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.

labels.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve VIII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VIII, a sensory nerve from the ear that enters where the pons meets the medulla. One part carries hearing and the other carries balance: the position and movement of the head.

labels.name: Glossopharyngeal nerve IX
labels.fn: Cranial nerve IX, a mixed nerve from the medulla. It carries taste and touch from the back third of the tongue and the throat, helps you swallow, and drives saliva secretion from the gland in front of the ear.

labels.name: Hypoglossal nerve XII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve XII, a motor nerve from the medulla that moves the tongue. When one side is damaged, the stuck-out tongue points toward the injured side.

labels.name: Vagus nerve X
labels.fn: Cranial nerve X, the "wandering" nerve from the medulla. It is the main parasympathetic nerve to the heart, the lungs and most of the gut, and it moves the muscles of the throat and voice box.

follow.q: Which cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic signals that slow the heart and speed digestion?
follow.why: The vagus nerve wanders from the medulla through the neck into the chest and abdomen and carries most of the body's parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs and gut. The glossopharyngeal and oculomotor nerves carry parasympathetic fibers only to glands and eye structures in the head, and the accessory nerve is purely motor to two neck muscles.

labels.name: Accessory nerve XI
labels.fn: Cranial nerve XI, a motor nerve whose rootlets come from the upper cervical spinal cord and rise through the foramen magnum into the skull before leaving it again. It moves the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, which turn the head and shrug the shoulders.

labels.name: Eyebrow
labels.fn: A ridge of short, thick hairs over the brow. It sheds sweat and falling particles to the side, away from the eye.

labels.name: Orbicularis oculi muscle
labels.fn: The ring of skeletal muscle inside the eyelids and around the orbit. It closes the eye, gently when you blink and tightly when you squeeze the eyes shut.

labels.name: Levator palpebrae superioris muscle
labels.fn: A thin muscle that runs from the back of the orbit into the upper eyelid. It raises the upper eyelid to open the eye.

follow.q: A patient cannot fully raise the right upper eyelid, but can still squeeze both eyes shut. Which muscle is most likely weak?
options: Orbicularis oculi, the ring muscle around the eye
Superior rectus, which turns the eye upward
Inferior oblique, which turns the eye up
follow.why: The levator palpebrae superioris lifts the upper eyelid, so its weakness leaves the lid drooping. The orbicularis oculi closes the eye, and it still works because the eyes squeeze shut. The superior rectus and inferior oblique move the eyeball, not the lid.

labels.name: Palpebral conjunctiva
labels.fn: The part of the conjunctiva that lines the inner surface of the eyelids. It folds back onto the eyeball as the conjunctiva that covers the white of the eye.

labels.name: Eyelashes
labels.fn: Rows of stiff hairs along the eyelid margins. Touching them sets off a blink, which keeps particles off the surface of the eye.

labels.name: Cornea
labels.fn: The clear, curved front of the fibrous tunic, continuous with the sclera. It has no blood vessels and does most of the eye's bending (refraction) of incoming light.

labels.name: Conjunctiva
labels.fn: A thin mucous membrane covering the white of the eye and lining the eyelids. It stops at the edge of the cornea and keeps the eye's surface moist.

follow.q: In conjunctivitis ("pink eye") the conjunctiva is inflamed. Which part of the eye's surface stays clear, because the conjunctiva does not cover it?
follow.why: The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye and lines the eyelids, but it stops at the edge of the cornea. Its tiny blood vessels swell in conjunctivitis and turn the white and the lid linings red, while the cornea, which has no blood vessels, stays clear.

labels.name: Superior oblique muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle whose tendon loops through the trochlea before attaching to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top inward.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: A small loop of cartilage ("pulley") at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The superior oblique tendon passes through it and changes direction toward the eyeball.

labels.name: Superior oblique tendon
labels.fn: The tendon of the superior oblique muscle. It passes through the trochlea, turns back and attaches to the top of the eyeball, so the muscle pulls from the front of the orbit.

follow.q: Why does the superior oblique pull the front of the eyeball down, even though the muscle itself lies along the top of the orbit?
options: It attaches to the lower surface of the eyeball
It starts from the floor of the orbit, below the eye
Its tendon turns through the trochlea at the front
It only works together with the inferior rectus muscle
follow.why: The tendon runs forward to the trochlea, turns back through it and attaches to the top of the eyeball behind its center. The pull therefore comes from the front inner corner of the orbit, which pulls the front of the eye down. The muscle attaches to the top of the eyeball and starts at the back of the orbit, not the floor.

labels.name: Superior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Lateral rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the outer side of the eyeball. It turns the eye outward, away from the nose; the abducens nerve (VI) supplies it.

follow.q: A patient's left eye cannot turn outward, away from the nose. Which muscle, and which nerve, is most likely affected?
follow.why: The lateral rectus is the only muscle that turns the eye outward, and the abducens nerve supplies it alone. The medial rectus turns the eye inward, the superior oblique turns it down, most strongly when it is turned in, and the inferior rectus turns it down.

labels.name: Common tendinous ring
labels.fn: A ring of tendon at the back of the orbit around the optic nerve. The four rectus muscles all start from it.

labels.name: Inferior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the bottom of the eyeball. It turns the eye downward.

labels.name: Inferior oblique muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the floor of the orbit under the eyeball to its outer side. It turns the eye up, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top outward.

labels.name: Superior rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: A small loop of cartilage ("pulley") at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The superior oblique tendon passes through it and changes direction toward the eyeball.

labels.name: Superior oblique
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle whose tendon loops through the trochlea before attaching to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top inward.

labels.name: Lateral rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the outer side of the eyeball. It turns the eye outward, away from the nose; the abducens nerve (VI) supplies it.

labels.name: Medial rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the side of the eyeball nearest the nose. It turns the eye inward, toward the nose.

labels.name: Inferior oblique
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the floor of the orbit under the eyeball to its outer side. It turns the eye up, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top outward.

labels.name: Inferior rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the bottom of the eyeball. It turns the eye downward.

labels.name: Posterior cavity (vitreous chamber)
labels.fn: The large space behind the lens, filled with the clear, jelly-like vitreous humor. The vitreous holds the eyeball's shape and presses the retina flat against the choroid.

labels.name: Superior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm)
labels.fn: A ring-shaped channel where the sclera meets the cornea. Aqueous humor drains into it and back into the blood; if drainage fails, pressure in the eye rises (glaucoma).

follow.q: The scleral venous sinus becomes blocked. What happens inside the eye?
options: Vitreous humor drains away and the eyeball softens
The lens stiffens and can no longer change its shape
The pupil stays wide open because the iris is squeezed
Aqueous humor builds up and pressure in the eye rises
follow.why: The ciliary processes keep making aqueous humor, which normally drains through the scleral venous sinus. If it cannot drain, the fluid builds up and pressure rises (glaucoma), which can damage the optic nerve. The vitreous humor is not drained this way, and lens shape and pupil size depend on muscles.

labels.name: Sclera
labels.fn: The tough, white outer coat of the eyeball (fibrous tunic). It protects the eye, keeps its shape and gives the extrinsic eye muscles an attachment.

labels.name: Suspensory ligaments
labels.fn: Fine fibers (zonule fibers) that run from the ciliary body to the edge of the lens and hold it in place. Their pull on the lens sets how round it is.

labels.name: Choroid
labels.fn: The dark, blood-rich layer of the vascular tunic between the sclera and the retina. It feeds the outer retina and absorbs stray light.

labels.name: Lens
labels.fn: A clear, flexible disc behind the iris, held by the suspensory ligaments. It changes shape to fine-tune focus for near and far objects (accommodation).

labels.name: Cornea
labels.fn: The clear, curved front of the fibrous tunic, continuous with the sclera. It has no blood vessels and does most of the eye's bending (refraction) of incoming light.

labels.name: Retina
labels.fn: The inner, neural tunic of the eyeball. It holds the rods and cones that turn light into electrical signals, and the neurons that send those signals out through the optic nerve.

labels.name: Iris
labels.fn: The colored ring of the vascular tunic in front of the lens. Its two sets of smooth muscle change the size of the pupil and so control how much light enters.

labels.name: Pupil
labels.fn: The opening at the center of the iris. Light passes through it to the lens; it narrows in bright light and widens in dim light.

labels.name: Fovea centralis
labels.fn: A small pit in the center of the retina, packed with cones and without rods. It gives the sharpest, most detailed color vision.

labels.name: Anterior cavity (contains aqueous humor)
labels.fn: The space in front of the lens, filled with watery aqueous humor. The iris divides it into the anterior and posterior chambers.

labels.name: Posterior chamber
labels.fn: The narrow part of the anterior cavity between the iris and the lens. The ciliary processes release aqueous humor into it, and the fluid flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber.

labels.name: Optic (II) nerve
labels.fn: Cranial nerve II. It is made of the axons of retinal ganglion cells and carries visual signals from the retina toward the brain.

labels.name: Anterior chamber
labels.fn: The part of the anterior cavity between the cornea and the iris. Aqueous humor fills it and drains out at its edge through the scleral venous sinus.

labels.name: Suspensory ligaments
labels.fn: Fine fibers (zonule fibers) that run from the ciliary body to the edge of the lens and hold it in place. Their pull on the lens sets how round it is.

labels.name: Central retinal artery and vein
labels.fn: The blood vessels that enter and leave the eye through the optic nerve and branch over the inner surface of the retina, supplying its inner layers.

labels.name: Ciliary body
labels.fn: The thickened ring of the vascular tunic around the lens. It holds the ciliary muscle and the ciliary processes, which make aqueous humor.

labels.name: Optic disc (blind spot)
labels.fn: The spot where the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye. It has no rods or cones, so light falling on it is not detected: the blind spot.

follow.q: Why is there a blind spot in each eye's field of view?
options: No rods or cones sit where the optic nerve leaves
The fovea packs too many cones to separate the image
The lens cannot bend light far enough to reach the back
The choroid's dark pigment blocks light at one point
follow.why: Axons from the whole retina gather at the optic disc and leave the eye there as the optic nerve, so that spot has no photoreceptors and cannot detect light. The fovea is the point of sharpest vision, not a blind spot, and the lens and choroid do not create a single unseeing point.

labels.name: Ciliary process
labels.fn: Folds on the inner surface of the ciliary body. They make aqueous humor, and the suspensory ligaments attach to them.

labels.name: Ciliary muscle
labels.fn: Smooth muscle in the ciliary body. When it contracts, tension on the suspensory ligaments eases and the lens rounds up to focus on near objects.

follow.q: You look up from a far-off sign to read your phone. What does the ciliary muscle do?
options: It relaxes, so the suspensory ligaments pull the lens flatter
It contracts, which widens the pupil to let in more light
It relaxes, so the cornea bulges and becomes more curved
It contracts; the ligaments slacken and the lens rounds up
follow.why: Near focus needs a rounder, stronger lens. Contracting the ciliary muscle draws the ciliary body toward the lens, which eases the tension on the suspensory ligaments and lets the elastic lens round up. Relaxing it does the opposite, for distant objects. Pupil size is set by the iris muscles, and the cornea's shape does not change.

labels.name: Inferior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the bottom of the eyeball. It turns the eye downward.

labels.name: Left visual field
labels.fn: Everything you see to the left of the point you are looking at. Signals from it end up in the right visual cortex.

labels.name: Right visual field
labels.fn: Everything you see to the right of the point you are looking at. Signals from it end up in the left visual cortex.

labels.name: Binocular field
labels.fn: The central part of the view that both eyes see at once. Comparing the two slightly different images gives depth perception.

labels.name: Visual field of left eye
accept: visual field of the left eye
labels.fn: The whole area the left eye sees on its own. It overlaps with the right eye's field in the middle.

labels.name: Visual field of right eye
accept: visual field of the right eye
labels.fn: The whole area the right eye sees on its own. It overlaps with the left eye's field in the middle.

labels.name: Pituitary gland
labels.fn: A small gland hanging from the underside of the brain on a stalk, sitting just below the optic chiasm. A growth here can press up on the chiasm and cut off vision to the sides.

labels.name: Optic nerves
labels.fn: The two cranial nerves II, one from each eye. Each carries every signal from its own eye's retina back to the optic chiasm.

labels.name: Optic chiasm
labels.fn: The X-shaped crossing where the two optic nerves meet, just above the pituitary gland. Fibers from the nasal (inner) half of each retina cross to the other side here.

follow.q: A pituitary tumor presses on the middle of the optic chiasm from below. Which loss of vision is expected?
options: Total blindness in the eye on the tumor's side
Loss of the left visual field in both eyes
Loss of the outer half of each eye's field
Loss of only the central part both eyes share
follow.why: The fibers crossing in the middle of the chiasm come from the nasal half of each retina, which sees the outer half of that eye's field. Pressing on them removes the outer field on both sides (bitemporal hemianopia). Blindness in one eye needs damage to one optic nerve, and losing one whole side of the field in both eyes needs damage behind the chiasm, in an optic tract or the cortex.

labels.name: Optic tract
labels.fn: The bundle leaving the optic chiasm on each side. Each carries the signals for the opposite half of the visual field, from both eyes, to the thalamus.

follow.q: The right optic tract is cut. What does the patient lose?
options: All vision in the right eye
The left visual field of both eyes
The right visual field of both eyes
The outer half of each eye's field
follow.why: Behind the chiasm, the right optic tract carries fibers from the right half of both retinas, and those halves see the left side of the world. Cutting it removes the left visual field in both eyes. Losing one whole eye would mean damage in front of the chiasm, and losing the outer fields of both eyes points to the chiasm itself.

labels.name: Lateral geniculate nucleus of thalamus
labels.fn: A relay nucleus in the thalamus. Optic tract fibers synapse here, and its neurons send the visual signals on to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

labels.name: Left visual cortex
labels.fn: The primary visual cortex at the back of the occipital lobe. Each side receives the opposite half of the visual field and is where visual perception begins.

labels.name: Right visual cortex
labels.fn: The primary visual cortex at the back of the occipital lobe. Each side receives the opposite half of the visual field and is where visual perception begins.

labels.name: Malleus
labels.fn: The first auditory ossicle, the "hammer". It is attached to the tympanic membrane and passes its vibrations to the incus.

labels.name: Incus
labels.fn: The middle auditory ossicle, the "anvil". It passes vibrations from the malleus to the stapes.

labels.name: Stapes (attached to oval window)
labels.fn: The last and smallest auditory ossicle, the "stirrup". Its footplate sits in the oval window and pushes vibrations into the fluid of the cochlea.

follow.q: In the middle ear, vibrations pass from the tympanic membrane through the ossicles in which order?
follow.why: The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane, the incus sits in the middle, and the stapes ends in the oval window, where it pushes on the fluid of the cochlea.

labels.name: Vestibule
labels.fn: The central chamber of the bony inner ear between the cochlea and the semicircular canals. It holds the utricle and saccule, which sense head tilt and straight-line acceleration.

labels.name: Auricle
labels.fn: The visible flap of the external ear, cartilage covered with skin. It gathers sound waves and funnels them into the ear canal.

labels.name: Vestibular nerve
labels.fn: The part of the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) that carries balance signals from the vestibule and semicircular canals to the brainstem.

labels.name: Cochlear nerve
labels.fn: The part of the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII) that carries sound signals from the cochlea to the brainstem.

labels.name: Round window
labels.fn: A membrane-covered opening between the middle ear and the cochlea, below the oval window. It bulges out when the stapes pushes in, so the cochlear fluid has room to move.

labels.name: Ear canal
labels.fn: The tube through the temporal bone from the auricle to the tympanic membrane. It carries sound to the eardrum, and its glands make earwax.

labels.name: Cochlea
labels.fn: The snail-shaped part of the inner ear. Its fluid-filled ducts and the spiral organ inside them turn sound vibrations into nerve signals.

labels.name: Eustachian tube
labels.fn: The auditory tube, running from the middle ear down to the throat. It opens when you swallow or yawn, so air pressure on both sides of the eardrum stays equal.

follow.q: A person with a head cold, whose auditory tubes are swollen shut, flies on a plane that descends. Why do the ears hurt?
options: Fluid from the cochlea leaks out into the throat through the tube
Outside pressure is higher and pushes the eardrum in
The three ossicles lock together and stop vibrating
Air escapes from the inner ear through the round window
follow.why: As the plane descends, cabin pressure rises. Normally swallowing opens the auditory tube and lets air into the middle ear to match. With the tube blocked, pressure outside the eardrum is higher than inside, so the eardrum is pushed in and stretched, which hurts. The cochlea, ossicles and round window are not what equalizes pressure.

labels.name: Tympanic membrane
labels.fn: The eardrum, a thin membrane at the inner end of the ear canal. Sound waves make it vibrate, and it passes the vibration to the malleus.

labels.name: Tympanic cavity
labels.fn: The air-filled space of the middle ear in the temporal bone. It holds the three ossicles and connects to the throat through the auditory tube.

labels.name: External ear
labels.fn: The auricle and the ear canal, ending at the tympanic membrane. It collects sound waves and channels them in.

labels.name: Middle ear
labels.fn: The air-filled tympanic cavity with the three ossicles. It passes vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and raises their pressure about 20-fold.

labels.name: Inner ear
labels.fn: The fluid-filled chambers inside the temporal bone: the cochlea for hearing, and the vestibule and semicircular canals for balance.

labels.name: Organ of Corti
labels.fn: The spiral organ: a strip of hair cells and supporting cells on the basilar membrane, with the tectorial membrane over it. It turns vibrations into signals in the cochlear nerve.

labels.name: Bony cochlear wall
labels.fn: The spiral of dense temporal bone that encloses and protects the cochlea's fluid-filled ducts.

labels.name: Scala vestibuli
labels.fn: The upper fluid-filled channel of the cochlea. It starts at the oval window, so pressure waves from the stapes travel along it first.

labels.name: Cochlear duct
labels.fn: The middle channel of the cochlea, between the scala vestibuli and the scala tympani. It holds the spiral organ with its hair cells.

labels.name: Tectorial membrane
labels.fn: A gel-like flap lying over the hair cells. The tallest stereocilia of the outer hair cells are embedded in it. When the basilar membrane moves, the flap slides across the hair cells and bends their stereocilia: the outer hair cells' directly, the inner hair cells' through the fluid it drags.

labels.name: Basilar membrane
labels.fn: The floor of the cochlear duct, on which the spiral organ sits. It vibrates with sound, and each spot along it vibrates most to one pitch.

follow.q: A high-pitched tone makes the basilar membrane vibrate most near which part of the cochlea?
options: The base, near the oval window, where it is narrow and stiff
The apex, far from the oval window, where it is wide and floppy
Evenly along its whole length, from the base to the apex
Only in the scala tympani, next to the round window
follow.why: The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base and wider and more flexible toward the apex. High frequencies make the stiff base vibrate most, and low frequencies travel on to the apex. That place code is how the cochlea sorts pitch.

labels.name: Scala tympani
labels.fn: The lower fluid-filled channel of the cochlea. It ends at the round window, where the pressure waves are released.

labels.name: Spiral ganglion
labels.fn: The cluster of sensory neuron cell bodies in the cochlea's bony core. Their fibers pick up signals from the hair cells and form the cochlear nerve.

labels.name: Cochlear branch of N VIII
accept: cochlear branch of cranial nerve viii
cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve
labels.fn: The cochlear part of cranial nerve VIII. Its fibers start at the spiral ganglion and carry hearing signals to the brainstem.

labels.name: Tectorial membrane
labels.fn: A gel-like flap lying over the hair cells. The tallest stereocilia of the outer hair cells are embedded in it. When the basilar membrane moves, the flap slides across the hair cells and bends their stereocilia: the outer hair cells' directly, the inner hair cells' through the fluid it drags.

labels.name: Tether
labels.fn: A fine link (tip link) joining the tip of each stereocilium to its taller neighbor. When the stereocilia bend, it pulls ion channels open.

labels.name: Stereocilia
labels.fn: Stiff, graded bundles of projections on top of a hair cell. Bending them toward the tallest opens ion channels and depolarizes the cell; bending them back closes the channels.

follow.q: Stereocilia on a hair cell bend toward the tallest one. What happens first?
options: The hair cell fires an action potential down its own long axon
The tectorial membrane releases neurotransmitter onto the nerve
The ion channels close and the hair cell hyperpolarizes
The tethers pull ion channels open and the cell depolarizes
follow.why: Bending toward the tallest stereocilium stretches the tethers, which pull ion channels open; positive ions flow in and the hair cell depolarizes, so it releases more neurotransmitter onto its nerve fibers. The hair cell itself has no axon, and bending the other way closes the channels.

labels.name: Hair cell
labels.fn: A sensory receptor cell with a bundle of stereocilia on top. Bending the stereocilia changes how much neurotransmitter it releases onto the nerve fibers at its base.

labels.name: Macula
labels.fn: A patch of hair cells and supporting cells in the wall of the utricle or saccule, covered by the otolithic membrane. It senses head tilt and straight-line acceleration.

labels.name: Utricle (cut)
labels.fn: The larger of the two sacs in the vestibule, drawn cut open here. Its macula lies roughly flat and senses tilt and forward-backward acceleration.

labels.name: Saccule
labels.fn: The smaller sac in the vestibule, next to the cochlea. Its macula stands upright and senses up-and-down movement.

labels.name: Endolymph
labels.fn: The fluid inside the membranous ducts and sacs of the inner ear, including the utricle and saccule. It bathes the tops of the hair cells.

labels.name: Macula
labels.fn: A patch of hair cells and supporting cells in the wall of the utricle or saccule, covered by the otolithic membrane. It senses head tilt and straight-line acceleration.

labels.name: Otoliths
labels.fn: Tiny crystals of calcium carbonate on top of the otolithic membrane. Their weight makes the membrane slide when you tilt your head.

labels.name: Otolithic membrane
labels.fn: The gel layer over a macula, weighted by otoliths. When the head tilts or speeds up, it lags and slides, bending the stereocilia beneath it.

follow.q: You tilt your head forward. What makes the hair cells in the macula respond?
options: Fluid rushing around a semicircular canal pushes the cupula over
Sound waves arriving at the oval window shake the macula
The weighted otolithic membrane slides and bends stereocilia
The utricle swells with extra endolymph and stretches its wall
follow.why: Otoliths make the otolithic membrane heavier than the fluid around it, so when the head tilts, gravity pulls it downhill and it bends the stereocilia beneath it. Fluid lag in a semicircular canal signals turning, and sound is handled by the cochlea.

labels.name: Hair cells
labels.fn: Sensory receptor cells of the macula. Their stereocilia reach up into the otolithic membrane, and bending them changes the signal sent down the vestibular nerve.

labels.name: Vestibular division of vestibulocochlear nerve
labels.fn: The vestibular part of cranial nerve VIII. It carries signals from the maculae and semicircular canals to the brainstem and cerebellum.

labels.name: Otolithic membrane
labels.fn: The gel layer over a macula, weighted by otoliths. When the head tilts or speeds up, it lags and slides, bending the stereocilia beneath it.

labels.name: Otoliths
labels.fn: Tiny crystals of calcium carbonate on top of the otolithic membrane. Their weight makes the membrane slide when you tilt your head.

labels.name: Hair cell
labels.fn: Sensory receptor cells of the macula. Their stereocilia reach up into the otolithic membrane, and bending them changes the signal sent down the vestibular nerve.

labels.name: Macula
labels.fn: A patch of hair cells and supporting cells in the wall of the utricle or saccule, covered by the otolithic membrane. It senses head tilt and straight-line acceleration.

labels.name: Cupula
labels.fn: A tall gel cap over the hair cells in the ampulla of a semicircular canal. When the head turns, the fluid lags and pushes it over, bending the stereocilia.

follow.q: You start spinning to the right in a desk chair. Which sensor detects it, and how?
options: The cupula, pushed over by fluid lagging in a canal
The macula, as the otoliths slide downhill with gravity
The basilar membrane, vibrating at a low pitch as you turn
The tympanic membrane, pushed by the changing air pressure
follow.why: When the head starts to turn, the fluid in the canal lags behind and pushes the cupula over, bending the hair cells' stereocilia. The maculae sense tilt and straight-line acceleration, the basilar membrane responds to sound, and the eardrum is part of hearing.

labels.name: Ampulla
labels.fn: The swelling at the base of each semicircular canal. It holds the ridge of hair cells and the cupula that sense turning of the head.

labels.name: Ampullary nerve
labels.fn: The branch of the vestibular nerve that leaves the ampulla. It carries the signals of the hair cells under the cupula to the brainstem.

hints.why: A note printed beside the drawing that names the cupula: it would give the answer away.

labels.name: Left chain ganglia
labels.fn: The row of sympathetic ganglia running beside the spinal cord on each side, from the neck to the coccyx and linked into a chain. Preganglionic axons from T1 to L2 enter it and synapse here, or climb or descend in the chain before synapsing, so every body level gets sympathetic fibers.

labels.name: Right chain ganglia
labels.fn: The row of sympathetic ganglia running beside the spinal cord on each side, from the neck to the coccyx and linked into a chain. Preganglionic axons from T1 to L2 enter it and synapse here, or climb or descend in the chain before synapsing, so every body level gets sympathetic fibers.

follow.q: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons leave the spinal cord only from T1 to L2, yet sweat glands in the skin of the neck and of the foot get sympathetic fibers. How?
options: Cranial nerves carry sympathetic fibers up to the neck and down to the foot
The adrenal medulla sends sympathetic axons out to the skin
Preganglionic axons climb or descend in the chain before synapsing
Neck and foot skin are both supplied from the celiac ganglion
follow.why: Preganglionic axons that enter the chain can run up or down it and synapse in a ganglion at another level, so the chain carries sympathetic output from T1 to L2 to every level of the body. Cranial nerves carry parasympathetic, not sympathetic, fibers; the adrenal medulla releases hormones into the blood rather than sending axons; and the celiac ganglion serves abdominal organs.

labels.name: Superior cervical ganglion
labels.fn: The largest and highest ganglion of the sympathetic chain, in the neck. Preganglionic axons climb the chain to synapse here, and its postganglionic axons supply the head: the eye (widening the pupil), the glands of the face and the blood vessels of the head.

follow.q: A tumor at the top of the chest damages the sympathetic chain in the neck on one side. Which sign would you expect on that side of the face?
options: A wide pupil on that side
Heavy sweating of that side of the face
A small pupil and a drooping eyelid
follow.why: The superior cervical ganglion supplies the head, including the muscle that widens the pupil and a small muscle that helps hold the eyelid up. Losing it leaves a small pupil, a slight droop and dry skin on that side. A wide pupil and heavy sweating are what sympathetic activity causes, not its loss, and the heart is not supplied from this ganglion alone.

labels.name: Greater splanchnic nerve
labels.fn: A nerve formed by preganglionic axons from about T5 to T9 that pass through the chain ganglia without synapsing. It runs down to the celiac ganglion, where the axons synapse on neurons that supply the upper abdominal organs.

labels.name: Lesser splanchnic nerve
labels.fn: A nerve formed by preganglionic axons from about T10 and T11 that pass through the chain without synapsing. It runs to the celiac and superior mesenteric ganglia in front of the spine.

labels.name: Celiac ganglion
labels.fn: A collateral (prevertebral) sympathetic ganglion in front of the spine, high in the abdomen. Preganglionic axons reach it through the splanchnic nerves, and its postganglionic axons supply the stomach, liver, pancreas and spleen.

follow.q: Where do the preganglionic axons in the greater splanchnic nerve synapse?
options: In the chain ganglion at their own level
In the wall of the stomach
follow.why: Splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic axons that pass through the chain without synapsing and end in a collateral ganglion in front of the spine, here the celiac ganglion. Synapsing in the chain is the route to the body wall and limbs, ganglia in the organ wall are parasympathetic terminal ganglia, and the dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neurons.

labels.name: Superior mesenteric ganglion
labels.fn: A collateral (prevertebral) sympathetic ganglion in front of the spine, just below the celiac ganglion. Its postganglionic axons supply much of the intestines.

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric ganglion
labels.fn: The lowest collateral (prevertebral) sympathetic ganglion, in front of the spine, low in the abdomen. Preganglionic axons from the upper lumbar cord synapse here, and its postganglionic axons supply the end of the intestines, the bladder and the genital organs.

labels.name: Eye
labels.fn: The eyeball. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion widen the pupil; parasympathetic fibers narrow it.

labels.name: Lacrimal gland
labels.fn: The tear gland, above the outer corner of the eye. It gets autonomic fibers from both divisions; the parasympathetic supply is what drives tear secretion.

labels.name: Mucous membrane of the nose and palate
accept: mucous membrane of nose and palate
labels.fn: The mucous membrane lining the nose and the roof of the mouth. Its glands and blood vessels are under autonomic control.

labels.name: Mucous membrane of the mouth
labels.fn: The mucous membrane lining the mouth. Its small glands and blood vessels are under autonomic control.

labels.name: Heart
labels.fn: The heart. Sympathetic fibers from the upper thoracic cord (T1 to T4), relayed in the chain ganglia, raise the heart rate and the force of each beat.

follow.q: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons that speed up the heart lie in which part of the spinal cord?
options: Upper cervical cord, C1 to C4
Upper thoracic cord, T1 to T4
Lower lumbar cord, L3 to L5
Middle sacral cord, S2 to S4
follow.why: The sympathetic outflow to the heart comes from the lateral horns of about T1 to T4; the axons synapse in the cervical and upper thoracic chain ganglia. The cervical and lower lumbar segments have no sympathetic preganglionic neurons, and S2 to S4 give parasympathetic output.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe. Autonomic fibers act on the smooth muscle and glands of its wall.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The muscular tube carrying swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. Sympathetic fibers reach it from the chain ganglia.

labels.name: Stomach
labels.fn: The stomach. Its sympathetic fibers come from the celiac ganglion, and sympathetic activity slows its movements and secretions.

labels.name: Abdominal blood vessels
labels.fn: The blood vessels of the abdominal organs. Sympathetic fibers from the celiac ganglion narrow them, which shifts blood away from the gut during fight or flight.

labels.name: Pancreas
labels.fn: The pancreas, behind the stomach. Its sympathetic supply comes from the celiac ganglion.

labels.name: Adrenal gland
labels.fn: The adrenal gland on top of each kidney. Its inner part, the adrenal medulla, gets preganglionic axons directly with no ganglion in between; its chromaffin cells act as postganglionic neurons and release epinephrine into the blood.

follow.q: Which organ receives sympathetic preganglionic axons directly, with no ganglion between the spinal cord and the organ?
follow.why: Preganglionic axons pass through the chain and the celiac ganglion without synapsing and end on the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, which act like postganglionic neurons and release epinephrine into the blood. The heart muscle, the stomach wall and the iris are reached by postganglionic axons from chain or collateral ganglia.

labels.name: Kidney
labels.fn: The kidney. Sympathetic fibers narrow its blood vessels, which lowers the blood flow through it.

labels.name: Bladder
labels.fn: The urinary bladder. Its sympathetic supply comes from the inferior mesenteric ganglion.

labels.name: Gonads
labels.fn: The testes or ovaries. They get sympathetic fibers from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar cord.

labels.name: External genitalia
labels.fn: The external genital organs. Their sympathetic supply comes through the inferior mesenteric ganglion.

labels.name: Skin
labels.fn: The skin. Sympathetic postganglionic fibers from the chain ganglia run back into the spinal nerves to reach its sweat glands, the arrector pili muscles and its blood vessels.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The spinal cord. Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in its lateral horns from T1 to L2, which is why the sympathetic division is called thoracolumbar.

follow.q: Why is the sympathetic division called thoracolumbar?
options: Its ganglia lie only in the chest and the lower back
Its preganglionic neurons lie in the spinal cord from T1 to L2
It supplies only organs of the chest and abdomen
Its nerves leave through the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae only after synapsing
follow.why: The name comes from where the preganglionic cell bodies sit: the lateral horns of the thoracic and upper lumbar cord, T1 to L2. The chain ganglia run from the neck to the coccyx, the division supplies the whole body including the head and skin, and the axons leave the cord before synapsing.

labels.name: Ganglion impar
labels.fn: The single ganglion where the two sympathetic chains meet and fuse in front of the coccyx. It is the lowest ganglion of the chain.

labels.name: Pons
labels.fn: The middle part of the brainstem. No sympathetic preganglionic neurons lie here; the sympathetic outflow starts in the thoracic cord.

labels.name: Medulla
labels.fn: The medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem. It holds centers that drive sympathetic output down the spinal cord to the lateral horns.

labels.name: Sympathetic chain ganglion
labels.fn: One ganglion of the row of sympathetic ganglia running beside the spinal cord on each side, from the neck to the coccyx and linked to its neighbors. Preganglionic axons from T1 to L2 enter it and synapse here, or climb or descend in the chain before synapsing, so every body level gets sympathetic fibers.

follow.q: A preganglionic axon enters the chain at T1 and synapses in a chain ganglion at the same level. Where does its postganglionic axon go next to reach the sweat glands of the skin?
options: Into the dorsal root and back into the cord
Down a splanchnic nerve to a ganglion in front of the spine
Into the ventral horn of the gray matter
Back into the spinal nerve through the gray ramus
follow.why: The postganglionic axon leaves the chain ganglion through the gray ramus communicans and joins the spinal nerve, which carries it out to the skin. The dorsal root carries sensory axons into the cord, splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic axons to collateral ganglia, and the ventral horn is inside the cord.

labels.name: White ramus communicans
labels.fn: The short branch carrying myelinated preganglionic axons from the spinal nerve into the chain ganglion. White rami exist only from T1 to L2, where the sympathetic preganglionic neurons are, and the myelin gives them their white color.

follow.q: Why are white rami communicantes found only from T1 to L2, while gray rami are found at every spinal level?
options: White rami carry sensory axons from the chest and upper abdomen only
Gray rami carry preganglionic axons that come down from the brainstem
The lumbar and sacral cord have no spinal nerves that could carry them
Only T1 to L2 has the preganglionic neurons that white rami carry
follow.why: White rami carry the myelinated preganglionic axons into the chain, and those neurons exist only in the T1 to L2 lateral horns. Gray rami carry postganglionic axons back out to every spinal nerve so that the whole body wall and limbs get sympathetic fibers. White rami are not sensory routes, the brainstem sends no preganglionic axons into the chain, and every level has spinal nerves.

labels.name: Spinal nerve
labels.fn: The mixed nerve formed where the dorsal and ventral roots join. Sympathetic preganglionic axons ride in it briefly before leaving through the white ramus, and postganglionic axons rejoin it through the gray ramus.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The spinal cord in cross section. The sympathetic preganglionic neuron's cell body sits in the lateral horn of the gray matter, and its axon leaves through the ventral root.

labels.name: Dorsal root ganglion
labels.fn: The swelling on the dorsal root that holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons. It is not an autonomic ganglion: no autonomic synapses happen here.

labels.name: Gray ramus communicans
labels.fn: The short branch carrying unmyelinated postganglionic axons from the chain ganglion back into the spinal nerve. It is found at every spinal level and brings sympathetic fibers to the sweat glands, arrector pili muscles and blood vessels of the body wall and limbs.

follow.q: Which structure carries unmyelinated postganglionic axons from a chain ganglion back into the spinal nerve?
follow.why: The gray ramus carries unmyelinated postganglionic axons, which is why it looks gray. The white ramus carries myelinated preganglionic axons into the chain, a splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic axons on to a collateral ganglion, and the dorsal root carries sensory axons into the cord.

labels.name: Spinal nerve
labels.fn: The mixed nerve formed where the dorsal and ventral roots join. Sympathetic preganglionic axons ride in it briefly before leaving through the white ramus, and postganglionic axons rejoin it through the gray ramus.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The spinal cord in cross section. The sympathetic preganglionic neuron's cell body sits in the lateral horn of the gray matter, and its axon leaves through the ventral root.

labels.name: Sympathetic chain ganglion
labels.fn: One ganglion of the row of sympathetic ganglia running beside the spinal cord on each side, from the neck to the coccyx and linked to its neighbors. Preganglionic axons from T1 to L2 enter it and synapse here, or climb or descend in the chain before synapsing, so every body level gets sympathetic fibers.

labels.name: Spinal nerve
labels.fn: The mixed nerve formed where the dorsal and ventral roots join. Sympathetic preganglionic axons ride in it briefly before leaving through the white ramus.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The spinal cord in cross section. The sympathetic preganglionic neuron's cell body sits in the lateral horn of the gray matter, and its axon leaves through the ventral root.

labels.name: Sympathetic chain ganglion
labels.fn: A ganglion of the sympathetic chain. Here the preganglionic axon passes straight through it without synapsing, on its way into a splanchnic nerve. (OpenStax prints 'spinal ganglion' on this label; the structure is the chain ganglion, not the dorsal root ganglion.)

labels.name: Prevertebral ganglion
labels.fn: A collateral sympathetic ganglion in front of the spine, such as the celiac ganglion. Preganglionic axons reach it through a splanchnic nerve without synapsing in the chain, and its postganglionic axons supply abdominal and pelvic organs.

follow.q: A preganglionic axon passes through a chain ganglion without synapsing and continues in a splanchnic nerve. Where does it synapse?
options: In the dorsal root ganglion beside the cord
In the ventral horn of the spinal cord
It does not synapse before reaching the organ
follow.why: Axons in the splanchnic nerves synapse in the prevertebral ganglia in front of the spine, such as the celiac ganglion. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory neurons, the ventral horn is inside the cord, and only the adrenal medulla is reached with no synapse on the way.

labels.name: Splanchnic nerve
labels.fn: A nerve of preganglionic sympathetic axons that pass through the chain without synapsing and run forward to a prevertebral ganglion in front of the spine.

labels.name: Hypothalamus
labels.fn: A small region at the base of the brain, below the thalamus. It links the nervous and endocrine systems: its neurons sense conditions such as body temperature and water balance and control the pituitary gland hanging below it.

follow.q: Why is the hypothalamus described as the link between the nervous and endocrine systems?
options: It is a gland in the neck with no nerve connections to the brain
It is part of the brain, and its neurons control the pituitary gland's hormone release
It releases every hormone in the body itself
It sends nerve signals straight to each endocrine gland, which then need no hormones
follow.why: The hypothalamus is brain tissue, so it receives nerve input, and its neurons control what the pituitary gland releases. It does not make every hormone, and most endocrine glands respond to hormones, not direct nerve signals from it.

labels.name: Pituitary gland
labels.fn: A pea-sized gland hanging from the underside of the hypothalamus in a small pocket of the skull. Its hormones control several other endocrine glands, so it is called the master gland, though the hypothalamus directs it.

labels.name: Thyroid gland
labels.fn: A butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the neck, wrapped around the front of the trachea. Its hormones set how fast most body cells use energy.

labels.name: Thymus
labels.fn: A gland in the upper chest behind the sternum, largest in childhood and shrinking after puberty. White blood cells of the immune defenses mature in it, and it releases hormones that help them develop.

follow.q: At what stage of life is the thymus largest and most active?
options: It stays the same size throughout life
follow.why: The thymus is large and busy in childhood, when the immune defenses are being built, and shrinks after puberty as fat replaces much of it.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: the airway running down the front of the neck into the chest. It is not an endocrine gland, but it is a useful landmark, since the thyroid gland wraps around its front.

labels.name: Adrenal glands
labels.fn: A pair of glands, one on top of each kidney. Each has an inner part, the adrenal medulla, that releases epinephrine in the fight-or-flight response, and an outer part that makes steroid hormones.

follow.q: Where are the adrenal glands?
options: On the back of the thyroid gland
Behind the stomach, along its curve
In the upper chest behind the sternum
follow.why: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys (ad- = near, renal = kidney). The organ behind the stomach is the pancreas, the gland behind the sternum is the thymus, and the small glands on the back of the thyroid gland are a separate set.

labels.name: Pancreas
labels.fn: An organ lying behind the stomach. It is both an exocrine gland, making digestive enzymes that drain into the intestine through a duct, and an endocrine gland: small clusters of its cells release hormones into the blood that control blood sugar.

follow.q: Why is the pancreas counted as both an exocrine and an endocrine gland?
options: It releases digestive enzymes through a duct and also releases hormones into the blood
All of its hormones travel through ducts to the stomach
It stores bile and releases it after meals
Its hormones act only on the pancreatic cells right next to the cells that release them
follow.why: An exocrine gland empties through a duct and an endocrine gland releases hormones into the blood. The pancreas does both: most of it makes digestive enzymes that leave through a duct, while small clusters of cells release hormones into its capillaries. Storing bile is the gallbladder's job.

labels.name: Uterus
labels.fn: The hollow, muscular organ in the female pelvis where a baby develops during pregnancy. It is not an endocrine gland; the ovaries on either side of it are.

labels.name: Ovaries
labels.fn: The female gonads, a pair of glands in the pelvis on either side of the uterus. Besides producing eggs, they release hormones that control the reproductive cycle and female body development.

labels.name: Testes
labels.fn: The male gonads, a pair of glands held outside the pelvis in a pouch of skin. Besides making sperm, they release the hormone that drives male body development.

labels.name: Tail of pancreas
labels.fn: The narrow end of the pancreas, reaching across the abdomen toward the spleen on the left side.

labels.name: Lobules
labels.fn: The small lobes that give the pancreas its bumpy surface. Each is packed with clusters of enzyme-making cells, with pancreatic islets scattered among them.

labels.name: Head of pancreas
labels.fn: The broad end of the pancreas, tucked into the curve of the first part of the intestine just past the stomach.

labels.name: Pancreatic islet
labels.fn: A small, pale cluster of endocrine cells (an islet of Langerhans) set among the enzyme-making tissue, with capillaries running through it. Its alpha cells release glucagon and its beta cells release insulin straight into the blood.

follow.q: Into what do the islet cells release insulin and glucagon?
options: A duct that drains into the intestine
The enzyme-making clusters around the islet
The capillaries that run through the islet
The spleen, which stores the hormones
follow.why: Islets are endocrine tissue: they have no duct. Their hormones enter the capillaries that run through each islet and travel in the blood to the liver and other target tissues. The duct carries the enzyme-making cells' secretions, not hormones.

labels.name: Plasma
labels.fn: The straw-colored liquid part of blood, which rises to the top when blood is spun and makes up about 55 percent of its volume. It is mostly water carrying dissolved proteins, nutrients, gases, wastes and hormones.

labels.name: Buffy coat
labels.fn: The thin, pale band between the plasma and the red cells in a spun tube, less than 1 percent of the blood's volume. It holds the white blood cells and platelets.

follow.q: A blood sample is spun in a tube. What makes up the thin pale band between the plasma and the red layer?
options: Plasma proteins that have settled out
follow.why: Spinning sorts blood by density. The red cells are densest and pack at the bottom, the plasma is lightest and rises, and the white blood cells and platelets settle in between as the buffy coat. Plasma proteins stay dissolved in the plasma.

labels.name: Hematocrit
labels.fn: The packed red cell layer at the bottom of a spun tube. The hematocrit is the percentage of the blood's volume this layer fills, normally about 37 to 47 percent in women and 42 to 52 percent in men.

follow.q: A man's blood is spun and his hematocrit is 30 percent. What does this mean?
options: 30 percent of his blood is plasma and the rest is red cells, which is normal
His buffy coat fills 30 percent of the tube
30 percent of his white blood cells are abnormal
Red cells fill 30 percent of his blood's volume, below the normal range
follow.why: The hematocrit is the share of the blood's volume taken up by packed red cells. The normal range for men is about 42 to 52 percent, so 30 percent means too few red cells for his blood volume. The plasma would be about 70 percent, and the buffy coat is always under 1 percent.

labels.name: White blood cells, platelets
labels.fn: What the buffy coat holds: the white blood cells, which defend the body against infection, and the platelets, cell fragments that help seal damaged vessels.

labels.name: Red blood cells
labels.fn: The red blood cells, the densest formed elements, which pack at the bottom of a spun tube. They carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.

labels.name: Multipotent hematopoietic stem cell (hemocytoblast)
labels.fn: The stem cell in red bone marrow that gives rise to every kind of blood cell. When it divides, one daughter stays a stem cell and the other becomes a myeloid or a lymphoid stem cell, depending on the chemical signals it receives.

follow.q: When a hematopoietic stem cell divides, one daughter cell stays a stem cell. Why does that matter?
options: It keeps the marrow from ever running out of stem cells
It lets platelets form directly from the stem cell
It means the marrow can only ever make one kind of blood cell
It stops the marrow from making new blood cells
follow.why: Blood cells wear out and must be replaced for life. Because one daughter of each division stays a stem cell, the supply of stem cells is kept up while the other daughter goes on to make blood cells of every kind.

labels.name: Myeloid stem cell
labels.fn: The stem cell of the myeloid line. Its descendants are the red blood cells, the platelets and most kinds of white blood cells.

labels.name: Lymphoid stem cell
labels.fn: The stem cell of the lymphoid line. Its descendants are the lymphoid white blood cells, the immune system's specialized defenders.

labels.name: Megakaryocyte
labels.fn: A huge bone marrow cell with a large, many-lobed nucleus. Pieces of its cytoplasm pinch off to become platelets.

follow.q: Which description of platelets is accurate?
options: Small whole cells, each with its own nucleus
Young red blood cells that have not yet lost their nucleus
Fragments of a large bone marrow cell's cytoplasm
follow.why: Platelets are not whole cells. They are pieces of cytoplasm that break off megakaryocytes in the red bone marrow, so they have no nucleus. They are formed elements, not dissolved proteins, and they are not young red cells.

labels.name: Platelets
labels.fn: Small fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm, with no nucleus. They circulate in the blood and help seal breaks in vessel walls to stop bleeding.

sets.title: The heart in the chest and its wall

labels.name: 1st rib
labels.fn: The first and shortest rib, just under the collarbone. The top of the heart's large vessels sits just below its level.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by rings of stiff tissue that carries air between the throat and the lungs. It runs down the chest just in front of the esophagus and above the heart.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart. After rising from the left ventricle as the ascending aorta, the aorta arches up, back and to the left over the pulmonary trunk, then runs down behind the heart.

labels.name: Thymus
labels.fn: A soft organ in the upper chest, in front of the large vessels leaving the heart. It is large in children and shrinks with age, when much of it is replaced by fat.

labels.name: Base
labels.fn: The broad upper end of the heart, where the large vessels enter and leave. Despite the name it is at the top: the heart sits upside down compared with a jar standing on its base.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The largest vein in the body. It carries blood low in oxygen from everything below the diaphragm (legs, abdomen and pelvis) up through the diaphragm into the right atrium.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The muscular tube that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. It runs through the mediastinum behind the heart and the trachea.

labels.name: Mediastinum
labels.fn: The central compartment of the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs. It holds the heart inside its pericardial sac, the large vessels, the trachea, the esophagus and the thymus.

labels.name: Arch of aorta
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart. After rising from the left ventricle as the ascending aorta, the aorta arches up, back and to the left over the pulmonary trunk, then runs down behind the heart.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood low in oxygen from the head, neck, arms and upper chest, entering the right atrium from above.

follow.q: Which chamber does this vessel empty into?
follow.why: Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium, the receiving chamber on the heart's right side. The left atrium receives the pulmonary veins, and the ventricles receive blood only from the atria above them.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide artery that leaves the right ventricle at the front of the heart's base. It splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry blood low in oxygen to the lungs.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The organ where blood takes up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The right lung is slightly larger than the left, because the heart bulges into the left side of the chest.

labels.name: Left auricle
labels.fn: The ear-shaped pouch of the left atrium, peeking out beside the pulmonary trunk. The rest of the left atrium lies at the back of the heart, where the pulmonary veins enter it.

labels.name: Right auricle
labels.fn: The ear-shaped pouch of the right atrium, lying against the root of the aorta. Inside, its wall is ridged with pectinate muscles.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The organ where blood takes up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The left lung is a little smaller than the right and has a notch that makes room for the heart, which sits more to the left.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The receiving chamber on the heart's right side, forming its right edge. Both venae cavae empty into it, and it passes blood down to the right ventricle.

labels.name: Right ventricle
labels.fn: The pumping chamber that forms most of the heart's front surface. It receives blood from the right atrium and pumps it out through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The pumping chamber that forms the heart's left edge and its apex. It receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it out through the aorta to the rest of the body. Its wall is the thickest of the four chambers.

follow.q: Which vessel carries blood out of this chamber?
follow.why: The left ventricle pumps blood out through the aorta to the rest of the body. The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, and the superior vena cava and pulmonary veins bring blood into the atria.

labels.name: Ribs (cut)
labels.fn: The ribs, cut away in this view to open the thoracic cavity. They and the sternum form the bony cage that shields the heart and lungs.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the two layers of serous pericardium. A thin film of serous fluid in it, about 15 to 50 mL, lets the heart slide as it beats; if fluid or blood fills it quickly, the heart cannot expand (cardiac tamponade).

follow.q: A stab wound lets blood collect quickly between the layers of the serous pericardium. Why does the heart pump less blood?
options: The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, so trapped blood squeezes the heart and it cannot fill
The blood dilutes the serous fluid, so the heart loses its lubrication and stops
The blood clots onto the myocardium and paralyzes it
The pericardial cavity opens into the pleural cavity, so the blood spreads and collapses the lungs
follow.why: The fibrous pericardium is tough and barely stretches. Blood that builds up quickly in the pericardial cavity has nowhere to go, so pressure around the heart rises and the heart cannot expand to fill. Less filling means less blood pumped out with each beat. This is cardiac tamponade.

labels.name: Apex of heart
labels.fn: The pointed lower tip of the heart. It points down, forward and to your left and rests on the diaphragm, which is why the strongest heartbeat is felt on the left side of the chest.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Edge of parietal pericardium (cut)
labels.fn: The cut edge of the pericardial sac that encloses the heart: a tough outer fibrous layer lined by the parietal layer of serous pericardium. It anchors the heart in the mediastinum and keeps it from overfilling.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the two layers of serous pericardium. A thin film of serous fluid in it, about 15 to 50 mL, lets the heart slide as it beats; if fluid or blood fills it quickly, the heart cannot expand (cardiac tamponade).

follow.q: A stab wound lets blood collect quickly between the layers of the serous pericardium. Why does the heart pump less blood?
options: The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, so trapped blood squeezes the heart and it cannot fill
The blood dilutes the serous fluid, so the heart loses its lubrication and stops
The blood clots onto the myocardium and paralyzes it
The pericardial cavity opens into the pleural cavity, so the blood spreads and collapses the lungs
follow.why: The fibrous pericardium is tough and barely stretches. Blood that builds up quickly in the pericardial cavity has nowhere to go, so pressure around the heart rises and the heart cannot expand to fill. Less filling means less blood pumped out with each beat. This is cardiac tamponade.

labels.name: Endocardium
labels.fn: The thin inner lining of the heart's chambers and valves: a simple squamous endothelium on a thin layer of connective tissue. Its smooth surface lets blood flow without sticking.

labels.name: Fibrous pericardium
labels.fn: The tough outer layer of the pericardial sac, made of dense connective tissue. It anchors the heart to the diaphragm and nearby structures and, because it barely stretches, keeps the heart from overfilling.

follow.q: Which layer is the outermost covering of the heart?
follow.why: From outside in: fibrous pericardium, then the parietal layer of serous pericardium, the pericardial cavity, the epicardium (the visceral layer, stuck to the heart), the myocardium and the endocardium. The fibrous layer is outermost, which is why it can anchor the heart to its surroundings.

labels.name: Myocardium
labels.fn: The thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle. Its contraction does the pumping, so it is thickest where the heart must push hardest.

follow.q: Which layer of the heart wall does the actual pumping?
follow.why: Only the myocardium is made of cardiac muscle, and only muscle can shorten and squeeze. The endocardium and epicardium are thin linings, and the fibrous pericardium is connective tissue that holds the heart in place.

labels.name: Parietal layer of serous pericardium
labels.fn: The serous membrane that lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium. It secretes serous fluid into the pericardial cavity and faces the epicardium across that thin space.

labels.name: Epicardium (visceral layer of serous pericardium)
labels.fn: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium: a thin serous membrane stuck to the outer surface of the heart, forming the heart wall's outermost layer. It faces the parietal layer across the pericardial cavity.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and chest to the right atrium, entering it from above.

follow.q: Blood from your right arm reaches the heart through which vessel?
follow.why: Veins above the diaphragm, including those of the arms, head and neck, drain into the superior vena cava, which opens into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning up, back and to the left over the pulmonary trunk. Beyond it, the aorta runs down behind the heart.

labels.name: Right pulmonary artery
labels.fn: The branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries blood to the right lung. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is low in oxygen.

labels.name: Left pulmonary artery
labels.fn: The branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries blood to the left lung. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is low in oxygen.

follow.q: What makes a pulmonary artery an artery?
options: It carries blood away from the heart
It carries blood rich in oxygen
It has valves along its length
It carries blood at low pressure
follow.why: Arteries and veins are named by direction, not by oxygen. The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs; that blood is low in oxygen, which is why "arteries carry blood high in oxygen" is not a safe rule.

labels.name: Ascending aorta
labels.fn: The first part of the aorta. It rises from the left ventricle, just past the aortic valve and behind the pulmonary trunk, before curving over as the aortic arch.

labels.name: Left pulmonary veins
labels.fn: The veins that return blood from the left lung to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, and the blood in them has just picked up oxygen in the lung.

follow.q: Where do the pulmonary veins empty?
follow.why: The pulmonary veins bring blood back from the lungs into the left atrium, which passes it to the left ventricle to be pumped to the body.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide vessel that leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It carries blood to the lungs.

follow.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?
follow.why: The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the atria pump only into the ventricles.

labels.name: Right pulmonary veins
labels.fn: The veins that return blood from the right lung to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, and the blood in them has just picked up oxygen in the lung.

labels.name: Auricle of left atrium
labels.fn: The ear-shaped pouch on the front of the left atrium. It adds a little extra room to the atrium, letting it hold more blood before the blood moves on to the ventricle.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The upper right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, plus the heart's own used blood, and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

follow.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?
options: The superior and inferior venae cavae
The left and right pulmonary arteries
follow.why: The venae cavae carry blood back from the body and open into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The lower left chamber and the heart's main pump. It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the whole body, which takes high pressure, so its wall is the thickest in the heart.

follow.q: For years, the pressure in a person's body arteries has been well above normal. Which chamber's wall thickens most?
follow.why: The left ventricle must raise its pressure above the pressure in the aorta before its valve opens. Higher arterial pressure means more work every beat, and muscle that works harder grows thicker.

labels.name: Right ventricle
labels.fn: The lower right chamber. It pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close and offer little resistance, so its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's.

follow.q: Why is the right ventricle's wall thinner than the left ventricle's?
options: It pumps only to the nearby lungs, which need far lower pressure than the whole body
It pumps less blood per beat than the left ventricle
It receives blood with less oxygen, so its own muscle is weaker and cannot grow as thick
Its wall is thinned by the pressure of the lungs pressing on it
follow.why: Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The difference is pressure: pushing blood through the short, low-resistance route to the lungs takes far less pressure than pushing it through the whole body, so the right ventricle builds less muscle.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The largest vein in the body. It returns blood from everything below the diaphragm (legs, abdomen and pelvis) to the right atrium, entering it from below.

labels.name: Apex
labels.fn: The pointed lower tip of the heart. It points down, forward and to your left and rests on the diaphragm, which is why the strongest heartbeat is felt on the left side of the chest.

labels.name: Aorta
labels.fn: The largest artery. It leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve and carries blood to every part of the body except the lungs' air sacs.
